title: Can I borrow on the valuation, not the price, to cover my subsale costs?
videoTitle: ASKING SEAN #214 | ADJUSTING SPA FOR MORE FINANCING
excerpt: A first-time buyer wants a Maluri subsale for RM245,000 but a loan on its RM280,000 valuation, to avoid using savings. Sean explains why banks lend on the SPA price, and what to do instead.

qa.asker: M, a viewer who wrote in by email
qa.context: M is a first-time buyer looking at a subsale apartment in Maluri listed at RM260,000, with a market valuation of about RM280,000. M doesn't want to use up savings on the 10% down payment and other costs, and hopes to negotiate the price down to RM245,000 while borrowing RM280,000, using the difference for the down payment, fees and renovation.
qa.question: Is it possible to borrow on the higher valuation so the purchase is effectively 100% financed, and how does the process work?
qa.quote: Maybe you cannot afford the property.
qa.answer: Not simply: banks lend up to 90% of the price written in the SPA, not the valuation, and every fee and tax follows that SPA figure too. If the down payment and costs would wipe out your savings, either save a little longer, look at EPF withdrawals or genuine full-financing schemes, or accept that the property may be beyond your budget for now.

reasons.title: The SPA price sets the loan
reasons.body: Stamp duty, legal fees and any RPGT are all calculated on the SPA price. Writing a higher price raises the owner's and buyer's costs, so owners often refuse, and any such arrangement depends on the bank's own valuation, the owner's written consent through the lawyers, and your income qualifying for the larger loan.

reasons.title: Valuations come from the bank
reasons.body: An agent's figure isn't enough: the bank asks its panel valuers, who may quote different amounts. Even a high valuation only helps if you qualify for the bigger loan.

reasons.title: A subsale needs about 18% in cash
reasons.body: Beyond the 10% down payment come legal fees, stamp duty and other charges, paid in stages over a six- to nine-month process. It's easy to lose track, so budget for the whole amount from the start.

reasons.title: Owning costs more than the instalment
reasons.body: Maintenance, repairs and building levies add up. If the instalment is well above what you'd pay in rent, and you're single with an uncertain future, renting and investing first may be the better path.

actions: Budget about 18% of the price in cash before committing to a subsale.
Check how much you could withdraw from EPF towards a purchase under the current rules.
Ask banks whether you qualify for any genuine full-financing scheme for first homes.
If buying would leave no emergency fund, set a savings target, such as another RM10,000 in six to eight months, before buying.
Have any unusual price arrangement checked by your own lawyer before signing anything.
qa.caveat: If the price is a rare bargain and you can live without savings for a year or two, buying now can still be your choice; Sean asks whether your health, family and sleep can handle that. Sean also stresses he is not an agent and sells no property.

sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #214. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in June 2023. EPF withdrawal rules have changed since, so check the current ones.
